 MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making

Junhao Shen Email: shen.junhao@outlook.com    Qing Zong Email: qzong@cse.ust.hk    Yue Guo Affiliation: LIGHTSPEED Email: zqzhang27@gmail.com    Zhanqiu Zhang Email: guoyiwen89@gmail.com    Yiwen Guo    Hong Cheng Email: hcheng@se.cuhk.edu.hkProject Page: mmdm-benchmark.github.io Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong Affiliation: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Affiliation: Independent Researcher
Abstract

System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision-model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.

1 Introduction

System-1 Decision Models make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a textual state in a single forward pass (TypeSafe AI, 2026; Microsoft, 2026), which support diverse applications, including text and intent classification, model and tool selection, and rubric-based quality scoring (Ling et al., 2026). Therefore, a rigorous and comprehensive evaluation of these models must account for the diversity and complexities of decision making in real-world scenarios.

Recent benchmarks have assessed decision models across diverse tasks and calibration criteria (Duan et al., 2026; Solka, 2026; Standhartinger, 2026). However, many existing evaluations draw heavily on widely circulated public benchmarks, making test-set contamination a central concern for benchmark validity (Oren et al., 2024). Moreover, real-world decisions often combine long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies. For example, a practically useful model needs to track the current agent state, determine whether an earlier approval remains valid, and select an eligible tool from a large catalog with heterogeneous prerequisites. These settings call for an evaluation that combines task breadth with new instances and explicit tests of these capabilities.

In this paper, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 questions for evaluating text-based System-1 Decision Models across realistic decision scenarios. It combines broad task coverage with explicit tests of context understanding, option discrimination, and logical consistency. Table 1 compares its scope with existing decision benchmarks.

Specifically, MMDM evaluates Hard Single-select, Hard Multi-select, and Soft-label questions, requiring a unique correct choice, the complete valid set, or a prediction matching the reference distribution over outcomes. These answer types capture practical requirements such as choosing the next actions, identifying all eligible tools, and assigning probabilities to rubric scores under uncertainty. Decisions can depend on agent states, action prerequisites, or relationships among options. In benchmark construction, source answers and contextual evidence ground rewrites of states, queries and distractors to reduce memorization-induced score inflation (Zhu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). We combine these adaptations with recompositions and newly constructed tasks. The resulting 16 categories span knowledge and comprehension, logic and constraints, agent and workflow decisions, and preference and rubric judgments. With 2–1,024 options and complete inputs of up to 64,817 tokens, MMDM also tests these capabilities across varied context lengths and option spaces.

As shown in Figure 1, our evaluation of 28 decision models reveals substantial differences across capabilities. Models that perform well on world knowledge still struggle with interdependent options, decisions subject to constraints, and complete multi-select recovery. These capabilities matter in agent workflows, where choices interact, actions have prerequisites, and several tools or skills may be valid for the current goal. Specifically, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 (Perplexity AI, 2026) achieves 78.75% Hard Single-select accuracy on world knowledge, compared with 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning. WeMM-JEV 27B (WeMM-JEV Team, 2026) achieves the highest Hard Single-select accuracy of 76.00%, while the highest Hard Multi-select accuracy is 36.81%, highlighting the challenge of recovering all valid options. Model rankings also differ between hard-answer accuracy and soft-distribution error, making both necessary to characterize decision quality.

Overall, our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce a multitask decision benchmark that combines fresh decision instances with long contexts, large option spaces, and interdependent options. Second, we provide a unified evaluation protocol for single-select correctness, multi-select completeness, and soft-label distributional fidelity, together with an open dataset and toolkit. Third, our evaluation reveals capability gaps that are not captured by previous decision-model benchmarks, including failures in joint consistency and complete multi-select recovery, providing concrete directions for future model development.

2 Related Work

System-1 Decision Models.

System-1 Decision Models produce structured probabilities over request-defined options in a single inference step. Jev introduces a typed decision interface and Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions, making probability quality a central training objective (TypeSafe AI, 2026). After this closed-source model, open implementations explore different ways to obtain these decisions from language-model backbones. SemIf reads logits for option tokens directly and supports shared-prefix reuse across queries (Lee, 2026). OpenJev learns a shared decision head over request-defined options, using supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning (Shen, 2026). Intern-Decision and H2O-Lightning extend typed decisions to multimodal inputs (Zhu et al., 2026; H2O.ai, 2026). Microsoft Decision-1 post-trains Qwen3.5-9B for single-pass scoring in routing, verification, and workflow control (Microsoft, 2026). Together, these approaches develop efficient readout, task adaptation, and probability calibration. Their growing use in software and agent pipelines makes it essential to evaluate whether they preserve decision quality when the relevant evidence, prerequisites, and options interact.

Benchmarks for Decision Making.

JevBench establishes an early comparison of typed decision quality, calibration, latency, and cost (Standhartinger, 2026). DecisionBench broadens applied coverage to 43 tasks with runtime-defined options (Solka, 2026), while ReflexBench separated raw model quality from workflow-policy effects (Navarro, 2026). DecideBench subsequently introduced 400 contrastive decisions to test sensitivity to answer-changing context (Yong, 2026). Jev Evaluation examined 37 existing datasets with frozen templates (Deußer et al., 2026), and JEVal expanded systematic evaluation across 36 datasets and ten domains (Duan et al., 2026). These tool kits improve coverage and comparability, but their main evaluations leave complete multi-select decisions underexplored. Additionally, broad source reuse also leaves a need for fresh decision instances Oren et al. (2024). Complementary resources target individual capabilities. AgentBench evaluates interactive agents (Liu et al., 2024). ToolBench evaluates tool-use tasks (Qin et al., 2024). LongBench and LongBench v2 studies long-context understanding in challenging realistic tasks (Bai et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025). MuSiQue evaluates multi-hop evidence composition (Trivedi et al., 2022). They provide valuable capability tests, while a common assessment of option selection and probability allocation across these settings remains necessary. MMDM addresses this gap by combining fresh decision scenarios, long inputs, and large option spaces with single-select, multi-select, and soft-label objectives.

3 The MMDM Benchmark

MMDM evaluates decision capabilities across diverse tasks through a shared state–query–options interface. First, we formalize the decision problems, answer types and evaluation objectives (Section 3.1). Then, we describe data collection and construction (Section 3.2). Finally, we present task coverage and dataset statistics (Section 3.3).

3.1 Task Formulation

Decision Instance. A decision instance consists of a state ss, a query qq, and an ordered set of options 𝒪\mathcal{O}. The state provides the evidence and current situation, the query specifies the decision to make, and each option oj=(aj,cj)o_{j}=(a_{j},c_{j}) contains a name aja_{j} and an optional criterion cjc_{j} describing its meaning or applicability. A decision model fθf_{\theta} maps these inputs to an option distribution

x=(s,q,𝒪),p=fθ​(x)∈ΔK−1,x=(s,q,\mathcal{O}),\qquad p=f_{\theta}(x)\in\Delta^{K-1}, (1)

where 𝒪=(o1,…,oK)\mathcal{O}=(o_{1},\ldots,o_{K}) and ΔK−1\Delta^{K-1} is the probability simplex, so pj≥0p_{j}\geq 0 and ∑j=1Kpj=1\sum_{j=1}^{K}p_{j}=1. Options are provided in each request, allowing their names, meanings, and number to vary beyond a fixed output vocabulary. Criteria may refer to other options, requiring the model to interpret the option set jointly with the state and query.

Answer Types. Each instance has a reference distribution π∈ΔK−1\pi\in\Delta^{K-1} with one of three answer semantics. We use 𝟏​[⋅]\mathbf{1}[\cdot] for the indicator function.

Hard Single-select specifies one correct option yy, such as the only tool that meets a request’s requirements. The model should assign this option the highest probability. The reference places all probability mass on it,

πj=𝟏[j=y].\pi_{j}=\mathbf{1}[j=y]. (2)

Hard Multi-select specifies a complete set GG of equally valid options, such as several tools that can each fulfill the same request. Every member must rank above every invalid option. Equal reference mass represents their equal validity,

πj=𝟏[j∈G]|G|.\pi_{j}=\frac{\mathbf{1}[j\in G]}{|G|}. (3)

Soft-label specifies how likely each outcome is under the uncertainty described in the state. For example, a tool call may succeed or fail because the service is intermittently available. If the stated service conditions imply a 70% success probability, the reference assigns 0.7 to success and 0.3 to failure. The model should match the probabilities of all outcomes, including less likely ones. For outcomes ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega and a rule rr mapping each outcome to an option index, the reference is

πj=∑ω∈ΩP(ω∣x)𝟏[r(ω)=j].\pi_{j}=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}P(\omega\mid x)\mathbf{1}[r(\omega)=j]. (4)

Scoring tasks use ordered options with numeric values, such as levels of report completeness. A known score gives a hard single-select reference; uncertain outcomes give a soft distribution over levels. The expected score summarizes this distribution on the rubric’s numeric scale. Appendix B.3 details label derivation.

Evaluation Metrics. Per-question correctness for the two hard-answer tracks is

asingle​(p,y)\displaystyle a_{\rm single}(p,y) =[py>maxj≠ypj],\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[p_{y}>\max_{j\neq y}p_{j}\right], (5)
amulti​(p,G)\displaystyle a_{\rm multi}(p,G) =[minj∈Gpj>maxj∉Gpj].\displaystyle=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\min_{j\in G}p_{j}>\max_{j\notin G}p_{j}\right]. (6)

Hard Single-select and Hard Multi-select Accuracy average these correctness values over their respective tracks, counting failed requests and boundary ties as incorrect. Higher accuracy is better.

Separation–Balance F-score (SB-F) combines separation from incorrect options with balanced support for the correct set. For N=|G|N=|G|, let μ=N−1​∑i∈Gpi\mu=N^{-1}\sum_{i\in G}p_{i} be the mean correct-option probability and b=maxj∉G⁡pjb=\max_{j\notin G}p_{j} the largest incorrect-option probability, with b=0b=0 if every option is correct. The separation component is

S⁡(p,G)=1N​∑i∈Gmax⁡(pi−b,0)max⁡(pi,μ)+b.S(p,G)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in G}\frac{\max(p_{i}-b,0)}{\max(p_{i},\mu)+b}. (7)

A summand is zero when its denominator is zero. Each correct option earns credit only above bb, and μ\mu prevents negligible probability from earning full credit. Correct-set balance is

B⁡(p,G)=(∑i∈Gpi)2N​∑i∈Gpi2,B(p,G)=\frac{\left(\sum_{i\in G}p_{i}\right)^{2}}{N\sum_{i\in G}p_{i}^{2}}, (8)

with B⁡(p,G)=0B(p,G)=0 when the correct set receives no mass. Their product defines

SB−F⁡(p,G)=S⁡(p,G)​B​(p,G).\operatorname{SB\!-\!F}(p,G)=S(p,G)\,B(p,G). (9)

SB-F lies in [0,1][0,1], with higher values better. We average per-question scores over all valid multi-select responses to show the performance.

Soft Brier measures error across the full reference distribution. Score nMAE measures expected-score error relative to the rubric range, using the numeric levels vjv_{j}. These per-question errors are

Brier⁡(p,π)\displaystyle\operatorname{Brier}(p,\pi) =∑j=1K(pj−πj)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{K}(p_{j}-\pi_{j})^{2}, (10)
escore​(p,π,v)\displaystyle e_{\rm score}(p,\pi,v) =|∑j=1Kvj​(pj−πj)|maxj⁡vj−minj⁡vj.\displaystyle=\frac{\left|\sum_{j=1}^{K}v_{j}(p_{j}-\pi_{j})\right|}{\max_{j}v_{j}-\min_{j}v_{j}}. (11)

Soft Brier and Score nMAE average Equations (10) and (11) over valid native responses in their respective tracks. Lower values are better for both.

3.2 Data Collection and Construction

Collection. We select public datasets and agent trajectories that support a concrete decision with explicit options and a checkable answer. Sources span knowledge, reading, reasoning, preferences, code, and agent interactions. For example, QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) and LongBench v2 (Bai et al., 2025) supply document-grounded questions, BIRD (Li et al., 2023) supplies database problems, and ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025) and ToolTalk (Farn and Shin, 2023) supply interaction histories. Source questions and annotations provide the basis for adaptation and verification.

Construction. We combine source-grounded adaptation with semantic recomposition and newly constructed tasks. For rewritten source instances, we retain the original answers and supporting evidence while reformulating the state, query, and distractors. Semantic and option-quality checks select the resulting instances. This strategy builds on evidence that benchmark rewriting can mitigate memorization-induced score inflation (Zhu et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025). Recompositions introduce decision questions grounded in source databases or agent histories. Executable mechanisms construct interacting options, constrained plans, state transitions, and rubric outcomes with computable answers. Across all three routes, distractors are designed around identifiable failure modes, such as applying an expired rule, confusing entities, or overlooking the prerequisite.

Validation and Selection. We verify answers using source evidence, executable checks, and model review appropriate to each construction route. Five-model majority screening is followed by independent human expert review of borderline cases. Both stages apply the same quality standards for distractors, answer leakage, duplicates, and source overlap. An option-only probe masks the state and query; instances with unresolved shortcuts are excluded. Appendix B details the review procedure and selection rules.

3.3 Task Coverage and Dataset Statistics

MMDM contains 5,448 questions across 16 task categories, comprising 4,112 Hard Single-select, 633 Hard Multi-select, and 703 Soft-label questions. The 663 Score questions include 35 with hard levels and 628 with soft targets. The collection covers 62 registered source identifiers and 80 category–subcategory combinations. Option sets range from 2 to 1,024 options, including 94 questions with more than 255 options. Complete inputs include the state, query, option names, and criteria. We measure complete inputs with the Qwen3.5-4B tokenizer from the Qwen family (Yang et al., 2025). Their median length is 827 tokens, the 95th percentile is 13,318, and the maximum is 64,817. These ranges support evaluation from common short decisions to long-document reasoning and large-catalog selection.

The categories connect knowledge and language understanding with decisions about evidence, rules, actions, and assessments. They cover world knowledge and reading comprehension; deductive, quantitative, and option-dependent reasoning; agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, and workflows; and preference, rubric, and emotion judgments. Figure 2 summarizes all categories and their answer types. Appendix A further elaborate each category and option-count distributions; Appendix F presents representative questions and model responses.

4 Experiment

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models. We evaluate 28 System-1 decision models and use Random as a heuristic reference. These models return option probabilities directly through a decision-scoring head or a single decoding step, without generated reasoning or adaptive thinking. They include hosted APIs and locally deployed checkpoints. Each model uses its supported context window and option limit, preserving the capabilities available in its released checkpoint or API. Appendix C.1 details model selection, deployment settings, and the Random reference.

Protocol and Metrics. The evaluator preserves the query and all option names and criteria, deterministically removing the middle of the state when the context budget is exceeded. Independent option sets exceeding a model’s option cap are divided into groups that fit the cap. Each request scores all options in a group together. From each group, the highest-probability option advances for single-select, and up to |G||G| highest-probability options advance for multi-select. This reduction repeats until the retained options fit one final request. Reference cardinality and gold identities are hidden from the model. Option-dependent and distributional tasks keep the entire option set without splitting; inputs exceeding the model’s option cap count as capacity failures. Grouped outputs contribute to hard selection metrics; full-distribution metrics use native responses. We use the metrics defined in Section 3.1. Hard accuracies retain every question in the corresponding track, including failed requests. SB-F, Soft Brier, and Score nMAE use native predictions. Appendix C.2 specifies token budgets, grouping, and failure accounting.

4.2 Overall Performance

Similar single-select accuracy can accompany very different probability quality. In Table 2, WeMM-JEV and KnowLine differ by less than one percentage point in single-select accuracy. Yet KnowLine has nearly half the Soft Brier error and less than one-third the Score nMAE of WeMM-JEV. A model that chooses the right option frequently can therefore still be a poor fit for applications that use its probabilities or expected scores.

Complete multi-select identification and probability support remain weak. The highest multi-select accuracy in Table 2 is only 36.81%, and every model has an SB-F below 0.20. This means that current models often fail to recover the complete set of valid options and to assign probability appropriately across them. Thus, improving multi-select decisions requires progress not only in finding all correct options, but also in representing their relative support reliably.

Expected-score accuracy and distribution fidelity favor different models. Jev achieves the lowest Soft Brier, while KnowLine achieves the lowest Score nMAE. GPT-6 Luna Decisions also has a lower Score nMAE than Microsoft Decision-1 despite a higher Soft Brier. This difference arises because the expected score compresses an entire probability distribution into a single value, allowing probability errors at different score levels to cancel out. Therefore, reporting both metrics shows whether a model predicts a useful final score and whether the probabilities behind that score are themselves accurate.

4.3 Performance by Task Category

Models struggle when several conditions must hold at once. WeMM-JEV leads Deductive Reasoning in Table 3, yet scores below 60% on Option Logic, Constraint Planning, and Workflow Decision. KnowLine shows the same contrast, with 86.0% on Deductive Reasoning but 54.6% on Option Logic and 48.5% on Constraint Planning. In these tasks, an option may look correct on its own but conflict with another option, a rule, or an earlier action. MMDM separates these requirements from deduction, exposing a weakness in joint consistency that the broad knowledge-and-reasoning score of JEVal does not isolate.

Similar overall accuracy can hide very different strengths across tasks. Table 3 shows that WeMM-JEV performs better on world knowledge and emotion recognition, while KnowLine is stronger on workflow decisions and policy handling. Models with lower overall scores can still lead particular categories. Quyet achieves the highest accuracy on Evidence Validation, while Mapika leads Emotion Recognition. These differences show why category-level results matter when selecting a model for a specific workload, since a higher overall score does not guarantee better performance on the capabilities that workload actually requires.

Strong routing performance does not guarantee strong agent decision making. GPT-6 Luna Decisions outperforms Jev and Microsoft Decision-1 on Intent Routing, but performs worse on Tool and Skill Selection, Agent State Tracking, and Workflow Decision. The largest gap appears in Workflow Decision, which requires the model to account for prerequisites and action order. This shows that routing correctly does not necessarily mean the model can also choose the right action from the current agent state or coordinate a multi-step workflow.

4.4 Confidence Calibration

Overconfidence appears at different operating ranges. Figure 3 compares five representative models using reliability curves and expected calibration error (ECE), where lower is better. Intern-Decision is overconfident in the middle of its range. OpenJev is closer to the diagonal there, but its highest-confidence bin averages about 0.97 confidence and 0.87 accuracy. Thus, this difference matters in deployment because the same confidence threshold may be reliable for one model but overly aggressive for another one when making decision.

Higher selection accuracy does not ensure better calibration. OpenJev has higher single-select accuracy than Intern-Decision in Table 2, yet Figure 3 gives it a larger ECE. Perplexity and Jev achieve the lowest ECE among the five representatives, while Microsoft Decision-1 has the largest error and remains below the diagonal through much of the moderate-to-high confidence range. The curves and aggregate errors together show why model selection should account for both how often a model is correct and how reliably its confidence reflects that correctness.

4.5 Context and Option-Space Scaling

Model rankings change between long inputs and large option sets. The two panels of Figure 4 reveal different scaling profiles. OpenJev outperforms Intern-Decision in every option-count bin, but falls below it once complete inputs exceed 8K tokens. At 8K–16K tokens, their accuracies are 15.5% and 34.5%, respectively; on 129–1,024 options, they are 26.0% and 8.3%. This reversal distinguishes performance on long-input workloads from performance on large-option workloads. MMDM measures both axes because success on one does not predict the model ordering on the other.

Large catalogs expose differences hidden by compact choices. In Figure 4, Jev and Microsoft Decision-1 differ by about seven percentage points on 2–4 options, but by more than 37 points on 129–1,024 options. Perplexity retains the highest accuracy in the largest option bin, although its advantage over Jev is much smaller there than on 9–16 options. Across the released workloads and the protocol in Section 4.1, the curves reveal both severe losses and changing relative advantages as the option space grows. A single aggregate accuracy would conceal these differences in the scale of decisions each model can handle.

4.6 Case Studies

Models can accept a workflow or report that conflicts with other evidence. In Figure 5(a), Perplexity V1.2 selects a workflow that approves a document before editing it. Publication requires approval of the final revision, so those later edits invalidate the certificate. Jev and Microsoft Decision-1 select a valid ordering. In Figure 5(b), Hazel’s report is false under the unique consistent interpretation, yet all three models rank it above at least one true report. The two cases expose errors in checking an option against history or other options, even when the relevant conditions are explicit.

Models struggle to translate a simple record-level defect into the correct score distribution. In Figure 5(c), eight of nine records satisfy every rubric criterion, while one record lacks a review stamp. A three-record sample receives the lower score only when it contains that record, which happens with probability one-third. However, Perplexity V1.2 and Jev assign more probability to the lower score, while Microsoft Decision-1 predicts the correct most likely score but still assigns the probabilities incorrectly. This example shows that even a simple scoring rule can lead to errors in both the predicted score and its probability distribution.

5 Conclusion

We introduced MMDM, a benchmark of 5,448 questions across 16 task categories for evaluating text-based System-1 Decision Models. With option sets ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs reaching approximately 64K tokens, MMDM tests decisions across both familiar requests and complex contexts. Its single-select, multi-select, and soft-label tasks assess whether models choose correctly, identify all valid options, and assign useful probabilities and scores. Our evaluation of 28 decision models reveals clear gaps between these capabilities and exposes dimensions of decision quality that are not captured by previous benchmarks. The strongest models vary across answer types and task categories. High single-select accuracy can accompany inaccurate probabilities, while deduction and routing strengths coexist with weaknesses in joint constraints and workflow decisions. Reliability curves and scaling profiles further distinguish confidence quality from accuracy and long-input performance from large-option performance. These findings direct progress toward checking interacting conditions, handling larger decision spaces, and producing probabilities that support reliable choices and scores. We release MMDM and its evaluation toolkit to make progress on these capabilities easy to measure and compare.

Limitations

MMDM has three main limitations. First, it focuses on text-based decisions defined by a fixed state, query, and option set. Extending MMDM to multimodal inputs and interactive trajectories would broaden its coverage of real-world decision settings. Second, multi-select questions are concentrated in option logic, constraint planning, workflows, and tool or skill selection, while most soft targets come from rubric scoring. These settings provide clear labels and verifiable target distributions, but broader evaluation of subjective judgments will require references that better capture variation across human assessments. Third, MMDM combines newly constructed tasks with source-preserving adaptations, recompositions, and rewrites. Although recompositions and rewrites introduce new decision requirements and contexts, prior exposure to the underlying public source material may still occur.

Ethics Statement

MMDM combines publicly available research data with newly constructed decision tasks. We cite the source datasets and document their contributions in Appendix B. Source materials remain subject to their original terms of use. The same appendix describes model-assisted construction, label verification, and targeted human review, including independent assessment and adjudication of disagreements. Our experiments evaluate model predictions from recorded or simulated inputs; they do not execute the tools or workflows described in the questions. We release the benchmark and evaluation toolkit, with source attribution, to support transparent and reproducible research.

Appendices

The appendices are organized as follows.
∙\bullet Appendix A reports input coverage and defines the tasks.
∙\bullet Appendix B describes data sources, construction, label derivation, and quality control.
∙\bullet Appendix C details decision models, the Random reference, capacity handling, and supplementary metrics.
∙\bullet Appendix D reports complete category results, matched cohorts, and reliability analyses.
∙\bullet Appendix E describes release artifacts and reproducibility.
∙\bullet Appendix F presents examples with saved model responses for all 16 categories.

Appendix A Input Coverage and Task Definitions

Classification and Coverage. Table A1 defines the 16 capabilities and links each one to its corresponding example in Appendix F. A category identifies the capability a decision requires; the answer type specifies whether the target is one option, a complete valid set, or a distribution. We measure input length using the full text seen by the model, including the state, query, option names, and option criteria. Each example is capped at 65,535 tokens. Among the 5,448 examples, 3,155 are shorter than 1K tokens, while 356 exceed 8K tokens, including 107 longer than 32K. The number of options ranges from 2 to 1,024. At inference time, the actual token usage can be slightly higher because model providers add their own request formatting and reserved tokens.

Decision Interfaces. Jev exposes three interfaces for different kinds of requests (TypeSafe AI, 2026). They specify what the model returns. The answer types in Section 3.1 specify what makes a prediction correct and how it is evaluated.

Choice compares named options. A support request might ask whether a ticket belongs to billing, shipping, or returns, with each option’s criterion defining its responsibilities. The response contains the selected option and a probability for every option. In MMDM, this distribution supports evaluation against a single correct option, a set of equally valid options, or a soft reference, according to the task’s answer type.

Noul answers a yes/no query, such as whether a message requests a refund. It returns the probability of yes; values near one favor yes, values near zero favor no, and values near one-half express uncertainty between them. The remaining probability belongs to no, giving the two-option distribution used in evaluation. A definite reference answer is hard single-select, while a reference that quantifies uncertainty is soft-label.

Score evaluates an input against ordered, descriptive rubric levels. For report completeness, these might range from missing required evidence to meeting every requirement. The response contains a probability for each level and their probability-weighted numeric score. MMDM evaluates both the level distribution and the expected score. Therefore, Scoring questions belong to the hard single-select or soft-label track, depending on whether the reference identifies one level or a distribution.

Appendix B Data Sources and Construction

B.1 Source Collection and Adaptation

Table A2 lists every public source represented in the release, its contribution, and the decision task obtained from it. We collect labeled questions, supporting documents, response comparisons, code and database problems, agent trajectories, and tool or skill descriptions. Table A4 describes the question families that we construct from explicit rules, state transitions, and outcome mechanisms. For source-grounded rewrites, the original answer and its supporting context serve as semantic anchors. We rewrite the state and query and rephrase or replace distractors, preserving the facts and relations needed to justify the answer. The semantic and option-quality checks in Appendix B.4 verify that the revised input supports the reference answer and that incorrect options remain plausible but invalid.

Knowledge, Language, and Document. Adaptations preserve task-relevant evidence and label semantics within the state–query–options interface. Knowledge and reading tasks retain the premises needed to distinguish the answer; multi-hop questions preserve the documents and links joining the required evidence. Entailment and moderation tasks express the source labels as named options with explicit meanings. Emotion tasks preserve the source text and the relevant emotion inventory. Preference tasks retain the compared responses and the criterion governing the comparison. A preference between responses remains a selection label; numerical annotations are used according to their original meaning.

Code and Database. Program tasks preserve executable code and its input or specification. Database tasks provide the relevant schema and database conditions. In the BIRD adaptation (Li et al., 2023), we derive a decision query from the target SQL semantics and execute every SQL option against the source database. Validation checks the required operation, the resulting records, and whether distinct options produce distinguishable outputs. An option-only similarity probe checks whether a response can be selected by superficial resemblance among SQL statements without using the query, which rules out some naive samples.

Retrieval and Freshness. Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., 2024) supplies retrieval-strategy decisions, while RetrievalQA (Zhang et al., 2024) supplies cases requiring a judgment about external retrieval. FreshQA (Vu et al., 2024) supplies stable, time-sensitive, and false-premise questions. Its adaptation provides an explicit evidence date and decision date, and asks whether the available evidence suffices, should be refreshed, or contains a premise that should be rejected. The target is tied to the dated evidence presented in the state.

Agent Histories and Skill Catalogs. At a decision point tt, the state is the observed interaction prefix h≤th_{\leq t}, and the query asks which tool or skill is appropriate next. The prefix ends before the target action. Options contain tool names and contracts or skill names and descriptions. The release includes 239 such decisions from ComplexFuncBench (Zhong et al., 2025) and ToolTalk (Farn and Shin, 2023), comprising 163 tool selections and 76 skill selections. Two separate DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) calls review the history and every option with labels hidden and option order changed. Acceptance requires agreement on present applicability and the complete valid set.

Catalog-based questions use task and environment descriptions from SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026), retrieval annotations from ToolRet (Shi et al., 2025), and skill descriptions from Graph of Skills (Liu et al., 2026). Generated requests introduce concrete goals and prerequisites grounded in these descriptions. An additional 31 questions are built from a collected directory of 10,798 skills with provenance preserved. For each question, we review every option for functional overlap and applicability to the current request; all valid options are included in the multi-select target. Original retrieval positives and packaged skills serve as reference candidates, while the expanded option set is independently reviewed to determine the labels.

B.2 Original Task Construction

We construct new decision instances by specifying a mechanism, computing its reference answer, and rendering its states and conditions as natural language. The mechanism determines which details affect the decision. Distractors implement plausible mistakes, including an omitted prerequisite, an expired authorization, a stale artifact, a confused entity, or a missed exception. The final families and their validation procedures appear in Table A4.

Interdependent Options and Constrained Plans. Logic tasks define propositions whose truth values depend on other propositions. We enumerate satisfying assignments and check them with an independent truth-table implementation. Single-select questions ask for the unique complete interpretation; multi-select questions ask for all true propositions under that interpretation. Global interpretation rules are stated in the state, and interdependent statements appear in option.criteria. We check entity references, quantifier scope, and natural-language statements against the formal propositions. Planning tasks evaluate complete proposed assignments against eligibility, scheduling, resource, and precedence constraints; all feasible plans remain valid options.

State Transitions and Workflows. State tasks reconstruct the current situation from events and tool receipts. Their mechanisms track goal scope, artifact versions, committed or rolled-back updates, evidence readiness, and execution failures. Transactional histories are checked both by folding the event sequence and by independent SQLite replay. Workflow tasks compare complete action sequences under prerequisites and revision-sensitive certificates. A simulator tracks state and content versions, while a separate checker verifies action positions and required orderings. Workflow option sets contain at most 128 sequences.

Scenario and Rule Composition. Additional original tasks combine policy conditions, evidence, tools, practical planning, and scoring in concrete scenarios. Compositional rule programs introduce thresholds, exceptions, authority levels, document versions, and joins between pieces of evidence. Natural-language renderings preserve the facts and rules that determine the computed answer. For tasks with finite uncertain outcomes, the state supplies the underlying weights, transition probabilities, or sampling process used to derive the reference distribution.

B.3 Answer Encoding and Label Derivation

The released input follows x=(s,q,𝒪)x=(s,q,\mathcal{O}) in Equation (1). Each option has a stable identifier ιj\iota_{j} that links its name and criterion to the reference label. The record also specifies its Choice, Noul, or Score primitive and, for Score, the numeric levels v1,…,vKv_{1},\ldots,v_{K}. The released field question stores the query, and option.criteria stores each option’s description. Labels, categories, provenance, and verification traces are separate from the model-visible input.

Hard Single-select and Hard Multi-select. A unique correct option yy is encoded as πj=𝟏[j=y]\pi_{j}=\mathbf{1}[j=y]. A complete set of equally valid options GG is encoded as πj=𝟏[j∈G]/|G|\pi_{j}=\mathbf{1}[j\in G]/|G|. The latter target records known set membership, and evaluation tests whether every member ranks above every nonmember. Source labels, executable constraints, or agreement-based review determine these references according to the construction route. A deterministic rubric score uses a hard label at the corresponding numeric level.

Soft-label and Score. For finite outcomes ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega and an answer operator r⁡(ω)r(\omega) mapping each outcome to an option index, the soft reference is

πj=∑ω∈ΩP(ω∣x)𝟏[r(ω)=j].\pi_{j}=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}P(\omega\mid x)\mathbf{1}[r(\omega)=j]. (A1)

For Score, option jj carries the numeric rubric level vjv_{j}. The reference follows the uncertainty explicitly specified in the task. Weighted finite worlds, state transitions, and sampling without replacement provide computable outcome probabilities.

The main Score family evaluates a common rubric over a subset of records. Records carry attributes such as signed handoffs, attachments, current templates, and review markers. For a uniform sample SS of size mm from a population of LL records,

πj=|{S:|S|=m,r(S)=j}|(Lm).\pi_{j}=\frac{\left|\{S:|S|=m,\ r(S)=j\}\right|}{\binom{L}{m}}. (A2)

Every criterion is evaluated on the same sample, preserving dependencies among the checks. Exact enumeration is cross-checked by an independent combinatorial calculation. This family contributes 598 questions. Across all families, the 703 soft questions comprise 628 Score and 75 Choice or Noul questions. Every distribution records all levels, including zero-probability outcomes; Score also records the numeric scale. Example F illustrates this construction.

B.4 Cleaning, Correction, and Verification

We initially collected 683,237 instances from public sources, retaining 669,135 after normalization and deduplication. We subsequently constructed 75,588 additional instances, producing a pool of 744,723 for selection.

Representation and Semantic Checks. We check unique item and option identities, complete option references, valid score scales, normalized nonnegative labels, and agreement between answer types and references. Source-parent and request-overlap checks compare related instances with registered training, replay, and evaluation records. Answers are checked against source evidence, execution, independent formal computation, or blind review. Repairs undergo the corresponding check again; unresolved failures are excluded.

Option Quality. We further check whether the options can be distinguished from the information available in the state and query, rather than from superficial cues. Distractors should reflect realistic failure modes, such as overlooking a prerequisite or choosing a tool with similar functionality but incompatible requirements. We also mask the state and query and ask whether the answer can still be guessed from option names or descriptions alone. Options with obvious shortcuts, copied answers, or weak distinctions are removed. For SQL tasks, we additionally check whether different queries are semantically equivalent and whether surface similarity reveals the answer.

Multi-model Screening. Candidate instances are screened by DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), GPT-6-Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) with high reasoning effort, Gemini-3.8-Flash (Google DeepMind, 2026), Qwen3.8-Max (Qwen Team, 2026b), and GLM-5.2 (Z.ai, 2026). Each model independently judges whether an instance meets the representation, semantic, and option-quality standards above. Four or five accept votes support automatic inclusion; a 3–2 vote sends the instance to human review, and fewer than three accept votes exclude it. This stage accepted 4,715 instances automatically and referred 928 borderline cases for human review.

Independent Human Review. Two reviewers independently assessed all 928 borderline cases under a common standard operating procedure (SOP). The SOP applies the representation, semantic, and option-quality standards above, using source evidence, verification traces, and option-only probe results from the earlier checks. Reviewers verify that the state and query support the reference answer, that all valid options are represented, and that distractors reflect plausible errors rather than superficial cues. Their initial decisions agreed on 97.3% of cases; a third reviewer adjudicated the remaining disagreements. Corrections underwent the corresponding semantic or executable checks before inclusion. Combining automatically accepted and human-reviewed instances produced the final 5,448 questions.

Appendix C Models and Evaluation Details

C.1 Decision Models and Random Reference

Table A5 lists the selected decision models, release references, and deployment settings. Selection requires direct option-probability output through a decision-scoring head or a single decoding step, without generated reasoning or adaptive thinking. The run settings record model versions, tokenizers, context budgets, service and output reserves, option caps, code versions, and grouping seeds. Decisio entries identify both the inference implementation and base checkpoint. Limits reflect the model and serving interface.

Random supplies a heuristic point of reference by assigning equal probability to all KK options. We report analytical expected accuracies of 1/K1/K for single-select and 1/(K|G|)1/\binom{K}{|G|} for multi-select under uniform random tie-breaking. Its uniform distribution is used to compute SB-F, Soft Brier, and Score nMAE. Random has SB-F zero on every released multi-select question, since each contains at least one incorrect option.

C.2 Protocol and Metrics

Context and Option Handling. For context budget BB, service allowance HH, and output reserve RR, the adapter preserves the query, all options, and their criteria. It keeps approximately equal token spans from the start and end of the state and recounts the serialized request against B−H−RB-H-R. Truncation preserves Unicode boundaries and inserts an omission marker. Runs record the provider or proxy tokenizer. Fixed-field overflow and provider rejection count as failures; grouped calls share the prepared state. All requests follow the protocol in Section 4.1. A supported catalog is evaluated in one call. An independent catalog above the option cap is reduced recursively, with each call presenting all options in its group alongside the same prepared state. The highest-probability option in each group advances for hard single-select. For hard multi-select, the evaluator uses N=|G|N=|G| both as the evaluation cutoff and as the maximum number retained from each group; neither NN nor the reference option identities enter model requests. The metric evaluates complete-set ordering at this reference cardinality. Option-dependent and distributional tasks retain the complete option set without splitting. If that set exceeds a model’s option cap, the request is recorded as a capacity failure.

Implementation and Averaging. Hard accuracies include all questions and count boundary ties, failed requests, and missing outputs as incorrect. The implementation treats probability differences of at most 10−1210^{-12} as ties. SB-F, Soft Brier, and Score nMAE use valid native outputs over the complete option set. Each Score error is normalized by that item’s rubric range.

Confidence Calibration. We also measure how well single-select confidence predicts correctness using expected calibration error (ECE) (Guo et al., 2017). For LL predictions partitioned into ten equal-width confidence bins ℬb\mathcal{B}_{b},

ECE=∑b=110|ℬb|L​|a¯b−u¯b|,\operatorname{ECE}=\sum_{b=1}^{10}\frac{|\mathcal{B}_{b}|}{L}\left|\bar{a}_{b}-\bar{u}_{b}\right|, (A3)

where a¯b\bar{a}_{b} is mean correctness and u¯b\bar{u}_{b} is mean maximum option probability in bin bb; empty bins contribute zero. Lower ECE indicates closer agreement between confidence and accuracy. Matched calibration analyses use the same single-select questions with valid, native, full-state predictions and unique maxima across the compared models.

Unified Model Output. Every decision model returns a probability distribution over the options supplied in its request. The answer-type annotation and reference number of correct options are not included in the model input. Thus, single-select, multi-select, and soft-label questions share the same prediction interface, without an additional prompt specifying the target answer type or set size. Reference labels are only used by the evaluator

Appendix D Additional Experimental Results

D.1 Results by Task Category

Table A6 extends Table 3 to every category with multi-select or soft-label questions. The two blocks distinguish exact multi-select accuracy from distributional error. Jev achieves the lowest Soft Brier in three of the six categories, while the strongest multi-select results vary across models and tasks.

D.2 Matched-Cohort Analysis

Table A7 compares the five representative models on shared questions. For each metric, we retain questions for which all five models produced valid, native predictions using the complete input. Calibration also requires a unique highest-probability option. With the questions and input handling held fixed, Perplexity V1.2 leads both hard-answer metrics, while Jev has the lowest Soft Brier and Score nMAE. The contrast between selection accuracy and probability quality therefore remains on shared inputs. On the shared single-select questions, Perplexity V1.2 exceeds Jev by 7.93 percentage points (95% CI [6.41, 9.44]), while Jev’s Soft Brier is lower by 0.0592 on the shared soft-label questions (95% CI [0.0515, 0.0661]). We estimate both confidence intervals from 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples of source-parent groups, computing item-weighted means within each resample.

D.3 Multi-select Results

Table A8 focuses on the four substantial multi-select categories for the same five models. All five perform best on Tool and Skill Selection, where options describe independently applicable capabilities. Option Logic, Constraint Planning, and Workflow Decision instead require resolving dependencies or validating complete plans, and their accuracies remain much lower. This contrast helps explain why a model’s overall multi-select score depends on the task composition.

Table A9 breaks down the same protocol by whether the complete option set fits the model’s option cap. Accuracy remains low on catalogs requiring recursive reduction. These larger catalogs differ across models because their caps differ, so Table A7 complements this breakdown with 523 shared multi-select questions evaluated in one call with the complete state and option set. The strongest result on this common cohort is 36.90%, showing that the multi-select difficulty persists without option reduction. SB-F complements exact accuracy by measuring the strength and balance of support for the correct set.

D.4 Multi-select Separation and Balance

We further examine the probability distributions behind these multi-select results. Table A10 reports SB-F, separation, and balance on 284 questions shared by all 28 decision models, with results also broken down by category.

Weak Separation. WeMM-JEV and Perplexity V1.2 have the highest SB-F (0.1905 and 0.1900, respectively), but excel on different tasks. WeMM-JEV is stronger on Option Logic and Constraint Planning, while Perplexity performs better on Workflow Decision and Tool and Skill Selection. We average each metric over questions for each model. The medians across models are 0.113 for separation and 0.862 for balance, while median correct-option coverage is only 37.8%. Models therefore often distribute probability evenly among correct options without separating them from incorrect ones. Jev illustrates this pattern, with average balance of 0.915 and separation of 0.137. OpenJev has stronger separation but lower balance. Jev’s category results make the distinction clearer. Its SB-F falls from 0.465 on Tool and Skill Selection to 0.022 on Option Logic, where balance remains high (0.973) but separation is low (0.023). The main difficulty in these questions is distinguishing interdependent true statements from false ones.

Coverage and Probability Margins. Table A11 examines these errors on the same 284 questions. A valid top choice satisfies maxi∈G⁡pi>b\max_{i\in G}p_{i}>b, where bb is the largest incorrect-option probability. Coverage measures the fraction of correct options above bb, averaged across questions. Probability differences of at most 10−1210^{-12} count as ties. GPT-6 Luna Decisions and Jev rank a valid option first on 184 and 181 questions, respectively, but place the entire correct set above all distractors on only 36 and 57. Recognizing one valid option thus frequently leaves other valid options behind.

Even when the full set is correctly ordered, the probability margin can be narrow. We define this as b≥12​mini∈G​pib\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\min_{i\in G}p_{i}, meaning that the strongest distractor receives at least half the probability of the weakest correct option. This occurs in 20 of Luna’s 36 successes and 43 of WeMM-JEV’s 110. Across all 28 models, the median proportion is 45.6%. SB-F captures this weakness in probability separation even when exact accuracy counts the prediction as correct.

D.5 Task Mechanisms and Input Scale

State Reconstruction. We compare three types of state-tracking question, each with 16 options, using native predictions from all five representative models on complete inputs. Jev and Perplexity answer all 47 artifact-version questions correctly, identifying outputs with the required source version, validation, and approval. Their accuracies fall to 8.3% and 16.7% on 24 transactional-state questions, which require applying an ordered sequence of transactions under revision, lock, and capacity constraints. On 100 goal-scope questions, which ask which instructions apply given their owner, workspace, and revision, Jev reaches 26.0% and Perplexity 75.0%. Median input lengths are 2,836, 4,252, and 1,800 tokens, respectively.

Length and Decision Requirements. Table A12 compares long-document comprehension and multi-hop reasoning within Reading Comprehension category, using the same input-length ranges. All questions have four options, and both Jev and Perplexity receive the full state. The two reading tasks have different accuracies within each length range, with each task represented by its own set of questions.

The large-option comparisons cover Tool and Skill Selection and Constraint Planning, holding option count and inference mode fixed. For the 512-option skill-selection and plan-comparison questions, option names and criteria account for 99.4% and 97.1% of input tokens, respectively. Thus, long inputs can require extensive option checking as well as state comprehension. The comparisons separate finding an applicable skill from checking whether a complete plan satisfies its constraints.

D.6 Task-Conditioned Probability Diagnostics

Confidence Across Tasks. We examine predictions with confidence at least 0.9 among the 3,537 shared questions in the reliability analysis. Jev is almost equally confident on retrieval strategy (mean 0.969 over 123 predictions) and contextual emotion (0.968 over 50), yet accuracy differs sharply, at 97.6% and 50.0%, respectively. OpenJev answers all 55 high-confidence SQL questions correctly, compared with 63.2% of its 38 high-confidence emotion questions. Thus, the same confidence threshold corresponds to different error rates across tasks. To capture this variation, we compute ECE separately within each task category using the same ten confidence bins, then weight the results by question count. This prevents overconfidence in one task from cancelling underconfidence in another. ECE rises from 0.054 to 0.106 for Jev, from 0.085 to 0.110 for Intern-Decision, and from 0.092 to 0.116 for OpenJev. Jev illustrates the opposing errors, with confidence exceeding accuracy by 38.6% on Emotion Recognition but falling below it by 29.0% on Workflow Decision.

Expected Scores and Their Distributions. We examine 596 sampled-rubric questions using native predictions from all five models on complete inputs. For predictions with nMAE at most 0.05, equivalent to an error of at most 0.2 points on the 0–4 scale, we measure distribution error using total variation, TV⁡(p,π)=12​∑j|pj−πj|\operatorname{TV}(p,\pi)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j}|p_{j}-\pi_{j}|. This is the probability mass that must be reassigned to match the reference. Jev meets this nMAE threshold on 190 questions and Intern-Decision on 111. Their mean TV errors remain 0.323 and 0.306, respectively. Thus, a close estimate of the expected score can still misrepresent the probabilities of individual score levels. Each question scores a random subset of records against four criteria. The expected total score depends on the four individual pass probabilities, while the full score distribution also depends on which criteria pass together. Using the exact pass probabilities, we construct an approximation that treats the criteria as independent. It preserves the expected score but produces mean Brier and TV errors of 0.0127 and 0.0690 across the 596 questions. This illustrates why accurate expected scores and accurate score distributions require different information.

Appendix E Reproducibility

The dataset is available on https://huggingface.co/datasets/shenjunhao/mmdm, and the evaluation toolkit is on https://github.com/mmdm-benchmark/mmdm. The repository’s quick-start guide provides installation steps and model configurations. The toolkit can download the dataset or read a local JSONL file, resume cached runs, and export predictions and metrics. The https://mmdm-benchmark.github.io/ hosts the leaderboard and documentation.
